title: How Jensen Huang's return as NVIDIA's CEO is going over in China
description:
In China, Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO is being met with a mixed reaction – as Beijing weighs whether it wants the US company's chips at all.

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST: Jensen Huang now has his job back at NVIDIA. Whether China should have access to NVIDIA's best computer chips - that debate is now back, too. And how is all this playing out in China? Well, we've reached NPR's Jennifer Pak in Beijing. Hi there.JENNIFER PAK, BYLINE: Hi.SUMMERS: Jennifer, you're there in Beijing. Tell us what you've been hearing from people.PAK: Well, from the general public, some say this whole saga of Jensen Huang's swift fall and sudden return is kind of like a microdrama. I don't know if you're familiar with these. These are super popular, kind of like soap operas. They're broken down into bite-size episodes, two to three minutes each, super fast pace. And just like a microdrama, this Huang scandal has had a lot of twists and turns.In China's tech circles, the views are split. I spoke to Du Chen, a technology media editor at Ifanr in Beijing. He says one group believes Huang's conduct raises serious ethical violations and shouldn't be in charge. While the other group, he says, are ones who have had business dealings with NVIDIA or interacted with Huang directly and indirectly.DU CHEN: (Speaking Chinese).PAK: This group, he says, generally trusts Huang's ability as the company's CEO and believes he would return, just not as fast as it happened, like 11 days.SUMMERS: It was really fast, yeah. Now, what about the allegation that China launched a spy operation targeting NVIDIA and Huang? Has there been much discussion about that?PAK: China's foreign ministry has denied these spy allegations. NPR has just heard that in the U.S., congressional staff have been briefed by American intelligence officials. And a person familiar with the matter said there is no evidence the woman who had an affair with NVIDIA chief Jensen Huang, named Alice Huang - of no relation - is a Chinese spy, though she is believed to have passed along information to the Chinese after the affair started.Now, here in China, there's surprisingly little talk on the ground, not just because of censorship, says Du, the Chinese tech media editor we just heard from earlier. He says people here don't believe that Alice Huang was a spy. They were photographed openly. As for allegations that she and her company, Megaspeed, helped to smuggle NVIDIA chips to China, well, Du doesn't know the specific details, but he says...DU: (Speaking Chinese).PAK: While many people in the West, he says, may have heard about this for the first time through the U.S. media, you know, about NVIDIA chips entering China through gray channels, these are not a secret in China at all, he says, especially within the tech industry.SUMMERS: Well, Jensen Huang has said that he wants to be able to sell chips directly to China. So I wonder, is there hope for smoother access to those high-end U.S. chips?PAK: Maybe among some Chinese AI companies, but the expectation among industry watchers I've been speaking to say Washington is likely going to tighten export controls, and it already has. Now, in Beijing, there's been conflicting messages coming from officials because on the one hand, officials have been criticizing the U.S. for these export controls. At the same time, when the U.S. does approve chips for sale to China, Beijing has told its companies not to buy them, to buy local.So to make sense of this, I asked Steven Hai, who is an assistant professor of technology entrepreneurship at the Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University. He says, think of China's central government not as a monolith.STEVEN HAI: They want normal global trade, but they want so-called, like, its own developmental strategy in the long run.PAK: So short- to medium-term, he says, China wants access to NVIDIA's high-end chips until it can build up its own replacement, something that Jensen Huang has wanted to avoid.SUMMERS: NPR China correspondent Jennifer Pak in Beijing, thank you.PAK: Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR.
